A WIC story

The work
of getting help

Food assistance can change a life.
Getting it is another story.

By Megan Quigley

Scroll to begin ↓

A new baby

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

My baby is here. He is crying. I am exhausted.

Everyone says to sleep when he sleeps. Apparently that is also when I’m supposed to do everything else.

Same baby. Same income. Same need for food. Now watch our lives split: in one, I get WIC. In the other, I never do.

✓ With WIC

A friend

Is that food stamps?

No—it helps with food for you and the baby. You can get WIC and SNAP.

Oh. I had no idea. Can you send me the number? 1

○ Without WIC

My friend explains WIC.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

Thank God she said something. WIC could help me buy food while I’m breastfeeding—and help feed him as he grows. 1

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

In my other life, that text never comes. I know about food stamps. We have Medicaid. WIC never comes up. 2

Getting through the door

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

I call the number to apply. Before my appointment, I need to gather a few things. First: my ID.

✓ With WIC
IDAddressMedicaid
○ Without WIC

Then my address and Medicaid information. Medicaid helps establish income eligibility. It doesn’t enroll me in WIC. 1

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

Now the appointment. Doing it by phone saves a trip, but I still need a stretch of time when I can talk. 1

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

I’m approved. While I’m fully breastfeeding, my package includes $52 a month for produce, plus other foods. Okay. That would help. 3

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

Meanwhile, I’m buying the same kinds of food without that help. All of it comes out of my own budget.

From one person to the country

Without WICWith WIC
56.1%of eligible people receive WICUnited States · average month, 2023

One text helped me get through the door. But my story is only one of millions. 4

Without WICWith WIC
56.1%of eligible people receive WICUnited States · average month, 2023

Across the country, WIC reaches about 56 of every 100 eligible people. The others qualify for help they aren’t receiving. 4

And the chance of getting that help changes depending on where you live. 4

In 2023, WIC reached 79.6% of eligible people in Vermont, 62.4% in New York, and 41.3% in Louisiana. 4

Those differences don’t tell us why people miss out. They do show that making help available is only the beginning. 4

A place to use the card

A rural New York grocery trip

21.5 milesone way · by road

Back in my kitchen, the list is getting longer. Being approved is one thing. Now I need a store where I can use the card. 5

This run from Keene Valley to Lake Placid is 21.5 miles each way. Now add the baby, the bags, and getting home again. 5

I can shop wherever works for me. But at the register, I’ll have to cover the whole bill.

Without WICWith WIC

Families beyond convenient WIC store access

Common scale: 0–100%

This isn’t just one long drive. Nationally, 40% of low-income families with young children live beyond convenient access to a WIC store. 6

Without WICWith WIC

Families beyond convenient WIC store access

Common scale: 0–100%

For a family in a city, that means going more than a mile. In the countryside, more than ten. Having a card doesn’t make the trip disappear. 6

Inside the store

✓ With WIC○ Without WIC
18 eggs?

I need dozen-size cartons.

At last, the store. I start with the foods on my WIC list: eggs, milk, peanut butter, fruit, and vegetables. 1

Eggs—but the carton has eighteen. I need dozen-size cartons. Back down the aisle to swap them.

I don’t have that list to follow. I’m checking prices instead, putting things back when the total gets too high.

Fresh fruit for now. Frozen vegetables for later. Those use my produce dollars; the milk and eggs use separate quantities. 1

The card will help pay for this food. Getting the right things into the cart is still work. Finally, I head to checkout.

✓ WIC pays$46.10

I pay$3.74

I’m stocking up on the foods WIC helps me buy. Two dozen eggs, bananas, and carrots go down the belt first. 7

Then peanut butter and three gallons of milk. The sizes match my benefits this time.

Apples and grapes. I’m buying enough to keep fruit in the kitchen for a while.

Broccoli and spinach for the freezer. Fresh and frozen produce together use $32.62 of my $52 allowance. 7

The pasta sauce and white rice aren’t covered. I decide to pay for those myself.

For this $49.84 shop, WIC pays $46.10. I pay $3.74. That leaves more of my own money for everything else. 7

The very same food would cost me $49.84 out of pocket. Without WIC, I have to decide what stays in the cart.

The gap between the card and the kitchen shows up in research, too. In this study, substantial produce benefits went unused in about three out of ten certification periods. 8

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

Another month ends. Then another. In both lives, the next big date on the calendar is his first birthday.

A birthday. Another deadline.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

One candle. A whole year of feeding him. In the life with WIC, another deadline arrives with the birthday.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

It’s time to renew. The appointment conflicts with work. I put the reminder aside.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

Tomorrow, I remember after the office closes. Then I have to check which documents need updating.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

I’m not deciding we don’t need the food. I’m deciding whether I can deal with one more thing today.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

This time, I call before the deadline. I find an appointment I can manage. We stay enrolled.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

He’s two. His appetite is growing. So are the grocery lists.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

He’s three. I know which foods work for us. But keeping WIC still means keeping up with appointments.

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

He’s four. His need for food hasn’t expired with the paperwork.

43.5%

I’ve kept coming back. How many families manage that? Researchers followed children who enrolled in 2013: fewer than half participated consistently through four and a half years. 9

Without WICWith WIC

Eligible people reached · 2023

Common scale: 0–100%

A newer national snapshot looks at separate age groups. WIC reaches 82.3% of eligible infants, but just 26.9% of eligible four-year-olds. 4

What all that work is for

Without WICWith WIC

The Healthy Eating Index

The whole pattern of eating
scored from 0 to 100

Those groceries add up. But do they change what children eat? Researchers looked beyond the bill, scoring the whole diet on a 100-point scale. 10

Without WICWith WIC

The Healthy Eating Index

Continued into year 3
compared with WIC in year 1 only

At age three, children who stayed in WIC into their third year scored 3.6 points higher than children who only received it in year one. 10

Without WICWith WIC

The Healthy Eating Index

Continued into year 3
compared with WIC in year 1 only

That’s a modest difference in overall diet quality, associated with staying connected to WIC. The years after infancy matter, too. 10

✓ With WIC
○ Without WIC

Back to Maya. The same fifth birthday in both lives. Five years of needing food—and two different experiences of paying for it.

Look back at everything it took. WIC made nutritious food more affordable. But the help depended on hearing about it, enrolling, reaching a store, finding the right foods, and managing to renew.

More families could benefit if getting started came with a direct referral, staying enrolled fit around work and caregiving, and shopping meant nearby stores, clear labels, and checkout support. Each is a place to remove some of the work.

Getting help should take less work.

Behind the story

Sources & methodology

Narrative and dialogue written for this project. Research, calculations, prices, and map data are documented below.

New York WIC: applying and using benefits

Income eligibility is only one component of WIC certification. See also New York WIC FAQs, MHHC’s current phone appointment options, and New York’s benefit-expiration guidance. Product illustrations are schematic.

Qualitative referral study · 2026

Ten participant interviewees recruited through a New Hampshire WIC agency; the broader study includes New Hampshire and Vermont staff. Interviews February–April 2024; 8 of 10 learned of WIC from family/friends. Not nationally representative.

USDA · 2023 eligibility and coverage

Tables 3.1, 3.5 and 3.7. Coverage = average-month participants divided by eligible people. 95% intervals: Vermont 65.1–94.2%, New York 61.0–63.8%, Louisiana 39.9–42.7%, national 54.5–57.6%. Age values are cross-sectional.

USDA · WIC retailer access, Table A.20

FY2022 retailers; 2015–2019 ACS low-income families with children under 5 are a proxy for WIC-eligible families. Convenient access is within 1 mile in urban areas or 10 miles in rural areas. Rounded table percentages used.

USDA · FY2026 produce allowance

October 1, 2025–September 30, 2026: $52/month fully breastfeeding; $26/month child. Illustration assumes 12 fully breastfeeding months plus 48 child months, continuous eligibility and constant FY2026 rates. Excludes other foods and the optional juice substitution. Not actual redemption, total WIC value, guaranteed savings, or forecast.

JAMA Network Open · benefit redemption

Southern California, November 2019–June 2023 records; children aged 0–3 at certification in November 2019–June 2022. 188,368 participants. Table 2: 254,506 of 365,738 fruit-and-vegetable certification periods redeemed at least 70% (69.6%); the complement is 30.4%. Unit is certification periods, not people or lost dollars.

USDA · Infant and Toddler Feeding Practices Study, Year 5

2013 enrollment cohort. Consistent participation refers to mother or child receipt during years 1 and 2 and subsequent observed months through 54 months. Weighted 43.5% consistent, 56.5% not consistent. Not a current national count or a renewal dropout estimate.

Borger et al. · WIC participation and diet quality

Adjusted observational comparison at age 3: participation in only the first year was associated with a 3.6-point lower Healthy Eating Index–2015 score than participation into the third year. Scale is 0–100. Does not establish causation.

The stock-up basket · prices and WIC rules

Walmart online listing snapshots accessed September 24–25, 2026. Total $49.84; eligible foods $46.10; own payment $3.74. Quantities are for a larger stock-up with pantry food already at home, not a nutritionally complete meal plan. Prices are not a local store quote. The linked ledger contains every item, quantity, unit price, product source, and food rule. This is a WIC-focused basket rather than a full food budget: $32.62 produce (below the $52 breastfeeding allowance), two dozen eggs, three gallons of 1% milk and one 16 oz peanut butter jar. Covered amounts assume sufficient corresponding benefits and an authorized store. Frozen vegetable prices verified on Walmart product listings September 25, 2026; approved categories cross-checked against the NY March 2026 frozen-food list.

Artwork & approach

Original SVG character, environment, food, and chart drawings; AI-generated home illustration; OpenStreetMap road geometry; scroll-driven movement and receipt calculations. Inspired by character continuity in The Pudding’s Teenagers, conversational pacing in Middle School, and transaction-to-population storytelling in Yard Sale.
